stem: A client previously treated for colorectal cancer asks why carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels are being measured serially during follow-up. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Serial CEA measurements can help monitor treatment effect or raise concern for recurrence, but results must be interpreted with the rest of the clinical evaluation.
options.B: A single elevated CEA level definitively proves that colorectal cancer has recurred and makes further evaluation unnecessary.
options.C: CEA testing replaces all imaging and other follow-up assessments once treatment for colorectal cancer is completed.
options.D: CEA is used mainly to determine whether a person without cancer will develop colorectal cancer in the future.

rationale: NCI lists CEA as a blood tumor marker used in colorectal cancer to assess treatment effect and detect recurrence. NCI also explains that serial tumor-marker measurements during and after treatment can provide information about treatment response or possible recurrence. Tumor-marker results are not interpreted in isolation; changes require correlation with the client's history, examination, imaging, and other diagnostic information as clinically indicated. A single abnormal value does not by itself establish recurrent cancer or replace the rest of surveillance.
educational_objective: Explain the role and limitation of serial CEA testing in colorectal cancer follow-up: it can support monitoring for treatment response or recurrence but is not a stand-alone diagnostic test.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the original broad tumor-marker item into a CEA-specific colorectal-cancer surveillance scenario. Removed class-wide generalizations across markers with different indications, replaced the generic ASCO source with current NCI tumor-marker resources, and explicitly prevented the unsafe inference that a single abnormal marker establishes recurrence or replaces other surveillance methods.
audit_findings: Original item grouped CEA and CA-125 under one generic rule even though tumor-marker indications and interpretation differ by marker and cancer type.
Fresh NCI review directly supports serial CEA use in colorectal cancer to assess treatment effect and detect recurrence.
The final item explicitly excludes stand-alone diagnosis from one elevated value and preserves the need for correlation with the broader clinical evaluation.
The Reduction of Risk Potential mapping remains appropriate because the item tests surveillance and interpretation of a laboratory finding for recurrence risk.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct explanation with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, unsupported marker generalization, or unresolved source conflict.
